Yassamin Ansari>: \16\Clare McCann, Everything You Never Wanted to Know About the Education Department's 2019 Higher Education Rulemaking, New America (May 16, 2019), https://www.newamerica.org/education-policy/edcentral/ everything-you-never-wanted-to-know-about-the-2019-rulemaking/.
Risk-Based Reviews
Section 2(f) establishes a new risk-based review process for both accreditors and colleges. It would allow so-called ``high performing'' accreditors to have federal recognition for an additional three years without any Secretarial review. It would also allow accreditors to reduce compliance requirements for ``high performing'' colleges and programs. Together, these policies will lead to a serious lapse in oversight for the set of accreditors, colleges, and programs the Trump Administration deems as high-quality that may have concerning incidents arise while not under review. It does not make sense to loosen compliance requirements simply because an entity is able to meet said compliance requirements. A stronger approach to risk-based reviews could be to require the Department to conduct additional reviews of low-quality programs, colleges, and accreditors, which would ensure an increase in oversight for the most problematic actors. Public Member Requirements
Section 2(a)(4)(A) requires accrediting agency boards and governing bodies to have at least one public member representing the business industry for every six members. It also prohibits any member of trade associations or member organizations from serving as a public member. This would prohibit, for example, union trade association members from being involved in accreditation. This prohibition will needlessly restrict accreditors from having knowledgeable experts serve on accrediting agency boards, and has the extra bonus of applying to group the Majority has spent decades deriding.\17\
\17\E.g., John Knefel, Project 2025's extreme anti-labor agenda is an attack on unions and the entire working class, Media Matters for America, July 18, 2024, https://www.mediamatters.org/project-2025/ project-2025s-extreme-anti-labor-agenda-attack-unions-and-entire-working-class.
Prohibition on Additional Secretarial Oversight
H.R. 4054 takes away important oversight capabilities of the Department by limiting the Secretary's ability to intervene in various places within the accreditation process. Section 2(d) prohibits the Secretary from establishing any criteria for accreditors that Congress did not expressly authorize. Section 3(4) prohibits the Secretary from giving the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI) any additional functions established through regulations. Together, these policies will severely limit the Department's ability to make improvements to the accrediting agency approval and oversight process and safeguard federal student aid. The loopholes created by H.R. 4054's accreditation framework will take longer to mend as a result of this provision limiting the Secretary's authority.
H.R. 4054 UNDERMINES ACCREDITATION FOR RELIGIOUS INSTITUTIONS OF HIGHER
EDUCATION
H.R. 4054 allows religious institutions of higher education to evade accreditation standards for their programs of study and expands upon the complaint procedure in current law, while also tilting the process in favor of religious institutions in a way that makes it difficult for accreditors to provide meaningful oversight of academic programs at these institutions. In the end, H.R. 4054 will undermine accreditation of religious institutions of higher education and could leave students in the dark about whether their academic programs at these institutions meet standards for accreditation.
Religious institutions of higher education have long been part of our nation's higher education system.\18\ Data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) show that during the 2022-2023 Academic Year, 14.5% of U.S. institutions of higher education were religiously affiliated.\19\ Current law and regulations already require accreditors to give religious institutions deference with respect to their religious mission, but they still maintain the ability to ensure that religious institutions' programs of study meet core standards required for accreditation.\20\ For instance, the Higher Education Act (HEA) requires an accreditor to be consistent in applying and enforcing its standards for accreditation in a manner that respects the stated missions, including religious missions, of institutions of higher education.\21\ Further, current law also provides that, in the rare event that a religious affiliated institution loses its accreditation, the Secretary must allow a religious institution to maintain their eligibility for Title IV funding for a period of time sufficient for them to seek alternative accreditation should the Secretary determine that the reason for the loss of accreditation was either related to the religious mission of the institution or not related to accreditation standards.\22\

\19\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), Data Collection 2022 for Title IV-participating IHEs with a Religious affiliation.

Sec. Sec. 600.2, 600.11(d), 602.18(a).
\21\20 U.S.C. Sec. 1099b(a)(4)(A). Regulations also require accreditors to base any decisions on the standards of accreditation, without prejudice towards the institution's religious mission, but allows the accreditor to ``require that the institution's or program's curricula include all core components required by the [accrediting] agency.'' See 34 C.F.R. Sec. 602.18(b)(3).
\22\20 USC Sec. 1099b(k); It should be noted that religiously affiliated institutions also have the option to seek accreditation from a religious accrediting body if that more appropriately meets their needs. See Do Christian Colleges Have the Same Process as Public Colleges, Online Christian Colleges, https:// www.onlinechristiancolleges.com/faq/do-christian-colleges-have-the-same-accreditation-process-as-public-colleges/ (last visited September 12, 2025).
In 2019, the first Trump Administration issued a final rule (2019 Final Rule) related to a number of accreditation issues, including for religious institutions, under the negotiated rulemaking process required under the HEA.\23\ At the time commenters noted that the Department provided no evidence of any formal complaints made about an institution's negative treatment related to its religious mission during the accreditation process.\24\ The 2019 Final Rule required accrediting agencies to base accreditation decisions on an agency's published standards.\25\ It also required accreditors to respect an institution's religious mission-based policies in the areas of 1) curricula; 2) faculty; 3) facilities, equipment, and supplies; 4) student support services; and 5) recruitment and admissions practices, academic calendars, catalogs, publications, grading, and advertising.\26\ Importantly, the 2019 Final Rule was clear that an accrediting agency ``may require that the institution's or program's curricula include all core components required by the agency.''\27\ The regulations effectuated by the 2019 Final Rule remain in effect today. It is against this backdrop that the provisions of H.R. 4054 should be evaluated.
\23\Student Assistance General Provisions, The Secretary's Recognition of Accrediting Agencies, The Secretary's Recognition of Procedures for State Agencies, 84 Fed. Reg. 58834 (Nov. 1, 2019) (codified at 34 C.F.R. Parts 600, 602, 603, 654, 668, and 674.

Sections 2(a) and 2(g) give undue deference to religious institutions of higher education in such a manner as to compromise the integrity of accreditation of their programs of study and create a special complaint procedure for these institutions, making it nearly impossible for accreditors to provide meaningful oversight. Section 2(a) incorporates a portion of the language from the current regulations, which require accreditors to base any decisions on the standards of accreditation, without prejudice towards the institution's religious mission.\28\ However, Section 2(a) departs from current law stating that an accreditor may require a religious institution's program of study to include all core components required for accreditation but only if those requirements are not inconsistent with the institution's religious mission. This is in contrast to current regulations promulgated by the first Trump Administration which allow accreditors to require that an institution's program include all core components required by the accrediting agency without exception.\29\ Section 2(a) effectively creates a sweeping exemption that would allow religious institutions of higher education to skirt generally applicable and neutral accreditation standards for core curricula and program of study requirements by claiming those standards are not consistent with its mission. This not only threatens to undermine the accreditation process but could also harm students at these institutions who may reasonably believe that their program of study meets accreditation requirements since it's accredited.
\28\See 34 C.F.R. Sec. 602.18.
\29\See 34 C.F.R. Sec. 600.18(b)(3).
Section 2(g) reworks how a religious institution lodges a complaint against its accreditor, a change that could essentially undo the quality assurance aspect of accreditation altogether for such schools. Current law and regulations provide procedures to allow a religious institution to remain accredited after being sanctioned by its accreditor if the Secretary determines the sanction was ``related to its religious mission'' and not ``related to the accreditation criteria provided for in this section.''\30\ H.R. 4054 would turn this process on its head, creating the presumption that an accreditor's sanction of a religious institution was based on the institution's religious mission.\31\ Under H.R. 4054, it would be insufficient proof for the accreditor to claim it was applying a neutral and generally applicable rule in taking an adverse action against a religious institution. In response to a complaint, the accreditor must include in its response how the adverse action against an institution is based on violations of its standards and an explanation of how the adverse action does not fail to respect the religious mission of the institution in violation of Section 2(a) of the bill. The accrediting agency bears the burden of proof that its adverse action was not as a result of the institution's religious mission and that its ``action does not fail to respect the religious mission . . . by showing that the adverse action does not impact the aspect of the religious mission claimed to be affected in the complaint.''\32\ In reviewing complaints, the bill requires the Secretary ``consider the [religious] institution to be correct'' in its claims against an accreditor that its actions failed to respect the religious mission of the institution.\33\ If the Secretary fails to take action following a review of a complaint and the accrediting agency's response within the 30-day period, it shall be deemed as if the Secretary has determined that the adverse action by the accrediting agency failed to respect the religious mission of the institution.\34\ Taken together, the policies in Section 2(a) and (g) undermine the accreditation process by making it difficult for an accreditor to enforce a neutral standard that it applies to all academic programs against religious institutions' programs of study.
